The Pelagic armourhead (Pentaceros richardsoni) is a moderately large beryciform fish found over seamounts of the North Pacific, where it has been the subject of considerable fishery-related research. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been estimated at approximately 9.8% [GSI = approximately 9.8%] based on field sampling of mature individuals, at an ambient water temperature of 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C]. The ultimate total length attained by this species has been recorded at 56 centimeters [Li = 56 centimeters], a size that represents the upper limit observed in the oldest and largest individuals from archival catch data. In contrast, the total length at which females typically achieve puberty is substantially smaller, occurring at approximately 24 centimeters [Lp = approximately 24 centimeters], indicating a prolonged period of somatic growth following the onset of sexual maturation, a life-history pattern common among slow-growing, deep-dwelling teleosts.

At the earliest stages of development, the eggs of Pentaceros richardsoni are pelagic and undergo a relatively brief incubation period. Hatching occurs after approximately 4.9 days [ab = approximately 4.9 days] when the water temperature is maintained at 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C], a developmental rate that is consistent with the thermal regime of the species’ subarctic spawning grounds. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva is minute, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00021 grams [Wwb = 0.00021 grams], a value derived from the dimensions of the fertilised ovum, which measures roughly 1.1 millimeters in length and 0.6 millimeters in width. This modest initial mass places the species among the many marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, pelagic offspring as part of a high-fecundity, low-investment reproductive strategy. Following yolk-sac resorption, the exogenously feeding larva enters a planktonic phase during which rapid growth and morphological development occur before the transition to a benthic, juvenile existence.

As individuals progress through the juvenile stage, body mass increases substantially until the onset of sexual maturity. The wet weight at puberty for females has been estimated at 176 grams [Wwp = 176 grams], a mass that corresponds closely to the body size at which the total length reaches 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters]. This relationship between length and mass follows a power-law scaling typical of many benthic and demersal fishes. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males, representing the asymptotic body mass achieved by the largest, oldest individuals, reaches as high as 2,300 grams [Wwi = 2,300 grams]. This substantial difference between the mass at maturation and the maximum recorded adult mass underscores a life-history strategy in which males, and to a lesser extent females, continue to invest heavily in somatic growth well after reproductive capability is established, potentially enhancing competitive ability and reproductive output over a prolonged lifespan.

Under the thermal conditions typical of its environment at 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C], the maximum lifespan of Pentaceros richardsoni is notably extended for a teleost inhabiting temperate and subarctic waters, with the oldest documented individuals reaching an age of approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years], and hatching occurring after approximately 4.9 days [ab = approximately 4.9 days]. This extreme longevity, more typical of deep-sea or seamount-associated species, is accompanied by a correspondingly delayed schedule of maturation and reproduction. The total length at puberty of 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters] is reached only after several years of growth, a pattern that contrasts sharply with short-lived, fast-growing epipelagic species. The life-history syndrome of the pelagic armourhead, characterised by slow growth, great age, and large terminal body size, is similar to that observed in other pentacerotid fishes such as Pentaceropsis recurvirostris, from which some comparative reproductive data have been derived.

The gonadosomatic index of approximately 9.8% [GSI = approximately 9.8%] was recorded at 11.6 °C [T = 11.6 °C]. Such a growth trajectory, reaching an ultimate total length of 56 centimeters [Li = 56 centimeters] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight for males of 2,300 grams [Wwi = 2,300 grams], while achieving a wet weight at puberty of only 176 grams [Wwp = 176 grams] at a total length of 24 centimeters [Lp = 24 centimeters], highlights a pattern of delayed maturation that likely buffers population dynamics against environmental variability in the seamount ecosystem.
